mainTopic: Judges vouching for a colleague, ratifying a שטר with a full court, and when a woman is believed about her status (הפה שאסר and אמתלא)
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion about judges who vouch for a challenged colleague. The גמרא concludes that the challenge was about theft, and the judges are saying he did תשובה. Next, רבי זירא teaches that if one of three judges ratifying a שטר dies, the other two must write that three sat together. The גמרא then debates whether writing 'before us, the court' is enough, given that שמואל allows a בית דין חצוף of two. A new משנה follows: a woman who says she was married and is now divorced, or was captured but stayed pure, is believed, because הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר. Witnesses who know the problematic fact take that belief away. The גמרא looks for a Torah source and ends up assigning the words of the פסוק to other teachings. It then teaches that a woman who said 'I am married' and then 'I am single' is believed only if she gives an אמתלא, a believable reason, and it supports this with the story of a beautiful woman and a ruling of the חכמים in אושא. Finally, שמואל asks רב about a woman who said 'I am טמאה' and then 'I am טהורה,' and רב's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Neither kind of challenge seems to fit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a two-sided question: a theft challenge leaves two witnesses against two, and a family-lineage challenge is just 'revealing a matter.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is a theft challenge, it is two witnesses against two witnesses. If it is a challenge about a flaw in his family line, that is just revealing something that will come out anyway.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question about what kind of ערער (challenge) was raised against the judge. Each option seems to cause a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the challenge is גזלנותא (theft), the two witnesses who call him a thief and the two judges who call him fit cancel each other out, so nothing is settled. If the challenge is פגם משפחה (a flaw in lineage), that is only גילוי מילתא, a fact that will come out on its own and does not need real testimony. Then the judges could vouch for him even after signing with no problem, so that option does not explain the case either.

keyTerms.meaning: Two against two: two witnesses contradicted by two other witnesses
A challenge to someone's fitness
A flaw in family lineage
Merely revealing a fact; it does not need formal testimony

phrases.english: they are two against two.
phrases.notes: This finishes the first side of the question: if the challenge was about theft, it is two witnesses against two.

phrases.english: If it is a challenge of a flaw in family lineage,
it is merely a revealing of the matter.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּרֵי וּתְרֵי נִינְהוּ. אִי עַרְעָר דִּפְגַם מִשְׁפָּחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a two-sided question that began before this section
steps.kashyaTarget: The case where the judges vouch for their challenged colleague
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A theft challenge leaves two against two, so nothing is resolved. A lineage challenge is mere גילוי מילתא, so the judges could vouch for him even after signing. So neither option fits the case.

steps.title: A theft challenge, and the judges say he repented
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the challenge really was about theft. The judges do not deny the theft; they testify that he did תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, I will tell you it was a theft challenge. These judges are saying: we know about him that he did תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by choosing the theft option and explaining why it is not two against two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judges do not contradict the witnesses who said he stole. They add a new fact: he has since done תשובה. Since the two testimonies do not clash, there is no 'two against two' problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, I will tell you (the גמרא returns to an option it set aside and keeps it)
Theft or robbery, which disqualifies a person as a witness or judge
He repented

steps.whatToRemember: Testimony that a thief has since done תשובה does not contradict testimony that he stole, so it is not 'two against two.'

phrases.english: Actually, I will tell you
it was a challenge of theft,
and these ones are saying:
phrases.notes: 'These ones' are the other judges who are vouching for their colleague.

phrases.english: We know about him that he repented.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two-sided question by choosing the theft option
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines what the testimony is actually saying
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A theft challenge meant the judges flatly contradict the witnesses, two against two
steps.terutzMaskana: The judges admit the theft and add that he did תשובה, so there is no contradiction

steps.title: One of three ratifying judges died
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא teaches, in the name of רבי אבא, that if one of three judges ratifying a שטר dies, the other two must write that three sat together.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: I heard this from רבי אבא, and if not for רבי אבא of עכו I would have forgotten it. If three judges sat to ratify a שטר and one died, they must write: 'We sat as a court of three, and one is no longer here.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic starts. רבי זירא gives a rule for how to word a ratification when one of the three judges dies before signing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קיום שטר needs a court of three. If only two signatures appear, people might think only two judges ratified it. Writing that three sat and one has died shows the ratification was done properly.

keyTerms.meaning: To ratify a document by confirming the witnesses' signatures in court
In a sitting of three judges
He is no longer here

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule that a ratification must show a full court of three. The rest of the section builds on it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:

phrases.aramaic: הָא מִלְּתָא מֵרַבִּי אַבָּא שְׁמִיעַ לִי,
phrases.english: This matter, I heard from Rabbi Abba,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָאו רַבִּי אַבָּא דְּמִן עַכּוֹ, שְׁכַחְתַּהּ:
phrases.english: and if not for Rabbi Abba of Akko, I would have forgotten it:
Three who sat to ratify the document
and one of them died —
they must write:
"We were in a sitting of three,
and one is no longer here."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: הָא מִלְּתָא מֵרַבִּי אַבָּא שְׁמִיעַ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about how a ratification is worded
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If one of three ratifying judges dies, the other two must write that three sat and one is no longer here.

steps.title: Writing 'before us, the court' is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק adds that if the ratification says the שטר came 'before us, the court,' nothing more needs to be written.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: If they wrote in it, 'This document came out before us, the court,' they no longer need to add anything.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק adds to רבי זירא's rule. He gives a simpler wording that also works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain word בי דינא (court) is understood to mean a full court of three. So writing 'before us, the court' already shows three judges were present, even if only two signed.

keyTerms.meaning: This document
Before us, the court
No more is needed

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
And if he wrote in it:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁטָרָא דְּנַן נְפַק לִקְדָמַנָא בֵּי דִינָא —
phrases.english: "This document came out before us, the court" —
no more is needed.
phrases.notes: He means there is no need to add the line about three judges sitting and one being gone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: וְאִי כְּתַב בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a simpler wording that meets רבי זירא's requirement
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing 'before us, the court' shows a court of three, so nothing more is needed.

steps.title: Maybe it was a court of only two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: 'the court' might mean a בית דין חצוף of two judges. שמואל holds that such a court's ruling is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe it was an impudent court, as שמואל taught. שמואל said: two judges who judged, their ruling is a ruling, but they are called an impudent court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim that the word 'court' proves there were three judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to שמואל, two judges who rule still produce a valid ruling. They are only criticized as חצוף (impudent) for not using three. So two judges could call themselves 'the court,' and the word does not prove three were present.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps (introduces an objection)
An impudent court: two judges who rule without the required three
Their ruling is a valid ruling

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל does not say a court of two is invalid. Their ruling stands; they are only called 'impudent.' That is exactly why the objection works.

phrases.english: But perhaps it is an impudent court,
in line with Shmuel. As Shmuel said:
Two who judged, their ruling is a ruling,
except that it is called an impudent court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק's wording
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'before us, the court' proves there were three judges
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under שמואל, two judges can form a valid court, so the word 'court' does not prove three.

steps.title: The text names רב אשי's court
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ratification says 'the court of our teacher רב אשי,' which would follow the proper practice of three.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where it is written in it: 'the court of our teacher רב אשי.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב נחמן בר יצחק by saying the wording names the court of רב אשי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A known, established court like רב אשי's would be assumed to sit with three judges. So naming it removes the worry about a court of two.

keyTerms.meaning: Since it is written in it (the document)
Our teacher רב אשי

phrases.english: For it is written in it: "The court of our teacher Rav Ashi."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the בית דין חצוף objection
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case to a specific wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any 'court' might be just two judges
steps.terutzMaskana: The ratification names רב אשי's court, which follows proper practice

steps.title: Maybe רב אשי's court follows שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects again: maybe the חכמים of רב אשי's court themselves agree with שמואל and sat with only two.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the חכמים of רב אשי's court hold like שמואל!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming רב אשי's court helps only if that court insists on three. If its חכמים hold like שמואל, they might have sat with two, and the doubt comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים of רב אשי's court or study hall
They hold (this opinion)

phrases.english: But perhaps the Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi
hold like Shmuel!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא רַבָּנַן דְּבֵי רַב אָשֵׁי כְּדִשְׁמוּאֵל סְבִירָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that naming רב אשי's court proves three judges
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רב אשי's court holds like שמואל, it too might have sat with only two.

steps.title: רב אשי himself instructed them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the text adds 'and our teacher רב אשי said to us,' showing רב אשי himself guided the ratification.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where it is written in it: 'and our teacher רב אשי said to us.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final answer: the ratification says רב אשי personally instructed the judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the other חכמים of his court hold like שמואל, רב אשי himself was involved in this ratification. He would make sure it was done properly with three, so 'before us, the court' can be trusted here.

keyTerms.meaning: And he said to us

steps.whatToRemember: A ratification that says 'before us, the court' shows three judges only when the wording also rules out a court of two. Here that is done by naming רב אשי's court and saying רב אשי himself guided it.

phrases.english: For it is written in it: "And our teacher Rav Ashi said to us."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 7 and closes the discussion
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case further to an even more specific wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The judges of רב אשי's court might have acted as two, like שמואל
steps.terutzMaskana: רב אשי himself instructed them, so the ratification was done properly with three

steps.title: משנה: A woman who says she was married but is now divorced
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a woman who says she was married and is now divorced is believed, because the same mouth that forbade her also permitted her. If witnesses know she was married, she is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman who said, 'I was a married woman, and now I am divorced,' is believed. The mouth that forbade her is the same mouth that permitted her. But if there are witnesses that she was a married woman, and she says, 'I am divorced,' she is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that a woman is believed when the only source of the problem is her own statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without her words, we would not know she was ever married, so we accept the whole statement together. Once witnesses establish that she was an אשת איש, the problem no longer comes from her mouth. Her own claim of divorce is then not enough to remove it.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (the opening text being discussed)
The mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted
She is believed
A married woman
A divorced woman

steps.confusionAlert: She is believed only because nobody knew about the marriage except through her. Once outside witnesses know she was married, the rule of הפה שאסר no longer applies.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
A woman who said:
'I was a married woman'
'and I am divorced' — she is believed.
For the mouth that forbade
is the mouth that permitted.
phrases.notes: Her own words told us she was married, and those same words tell us she's free now.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם יֵשׁ עֵדִים שֶׁהָיְתָה אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ,
phrases.english: But if there are witnesses that she was a married woman,
and she says: 'I am divorced,'
she is not believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁאָמְרָה: ״אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ הָיִיתִי וּגְרוּשָׁה אֲנִי״ — נֶאֱמֶנֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of ratifying documents.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman is believed to say she was married and is divorced, because of הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר. If witnesses know she was married, she is not believed.

steps.title: משנה: A woman who says she was captured but remained pure
steps.stepSummary: The same rule applies to a woman who says she was taken captive but stayed pure. If witnesses know she was captured, she is not believed. If the witnesses came only after she married, she does not leave her husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she said, 'I was taken captive, and I am pure,' she is believed, because the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. But if there are witnesses that she was taken captive, and she says, 'I am pure,' she is not believed. And if the witnesses came after she married, she does not have to leave.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה applies the same rule to a שבויה, a woman who was taken captive. It then adds a special case where the witnesses arrive only after she is already married.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her claim to be pure is accepted when her captivity is known only from her own words. Witnesses to the captivity cancel that, so she is not believed. However, if she already married on the strength of her word before witnesses came, the משנה lets the marriage stand.

keyTerms.meaning: I was taken captive
Pure, meaning she was not violated in captivity
After she married
She does not have to leave her husband

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's rule is that a woman is believed when her own mouth is the only source of the problem. Witnesses who know the problematic fact remove that belief. However, a marriage that already happened before witnesses came is not broken up.

phrases.english: If she said: 'I was taken captive,'
'and I am pure' — she is believed.
phrases.notes: 'Pure' here means she was not violated while she was a captive.

phrases.english: For the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted.
But if there are witnesses that she was taken captive,
and she says: 'I am pure' — she is not believed.
And if the witnesses came after she married,
she does not have to leave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same principle from step 9 to a captive woman and adds the case of witnesses who came after her marriage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A captive woman is believed to say she is pure unless witnesses know she was captured. If those witnesses came after she married, she stays married.

steps.title: רב אסי brings a Torah verse as the source for the rule
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי derives הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר from the father's words 'I gave my daughter to this man as a wife.' The words 'to the man' forbid her, and the word 'this' permits her.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: Where in the Torah do we learn that the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted? From the פסוק: 'I gave my daughter to this man as a wife.' 'To the man' made her forbidden; 'this' made her permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by having רב אסי look for a source in the Torah for the משנה's rule. He finds it in a פסוק about a father speaking about his daughter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the father says 'I gave my daughter to the man,' he makes her forbidden to everyone, since she is now married to some man. When he adds 'this' and points to the husband, he makes her permitted to him. The same person who forbade her also permitted her.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
From where do we know?
From the Torah
He made her forbidden
He made her permitted

steps.confusionAlert: Here the father is the one speaking, not the woman. רב אסי uses the father's two words to show the idea that the one who creates the prohibition can also remove it.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rav Asi said:
From where do we know that the mouth that forbade
is the mouth that permitted, from the Torah?
As it says:
'I gave my daughter to this man as a wife.'
'To the man' — he made her forbidden,
phrases.notes: Saying she's married to some unnamed man makes her off-limits to everyone.

phrases.english: 'this' — he made her permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי: מִנַּיִן לְהַפֶּה שֶׁאָסַר הוּא הַפֶּה שֶׁהִתִּיר מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for the Torah source of the principle the משנה used.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The principle הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר is derived from the words לאיש and הזה in the פסוק.

steps.title: Why do we need a verse for something so logical?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב אסי: this rule is simple logic. The person who forbade her is the one permitting her, so no פסוק is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need a פסוק? It is logic: he forbade her, and he permits her!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב אסי's source. It argues the rule is obvious from logic alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we only know about the prohibition from someone's words, it makes sense to accept the rest of those words too. Since a סברא already teaches this, using a פסוק for it seems wasted. This forces the גמרא to find a different job for the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need a verse?
Logic, reasoning
He permits her

phrases.english: Why do I need a verse?
It is logic:
he forbade her, and he permits her!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רב אסי's derivation from the פסוק is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אסי's use of the פסוק as the source for הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rule that logic already teaches does not need a פסוק, so the derivation seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The verse teaches that a father is believed to forbid his daughter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the פסוק is really needed for רב הונא's teaching in the name of רב: a father is believed to make his daughter forbidden, learned from 'I gave my daughter to the man.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק is needed for what רב הונא said in the name of רב. רב הונא said in the name of רב: Where in the Torah do we learn that a father is believed to make his daughter forbidden? From the פסוק: 'I gave my daughter to the man.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the פסוק a new job. It does not teach הפה שאסר, which is logical. It teaches that a father is believed when he says his daughter is married.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making a woman forbidden to everyone with just one person's word is a big step that logic alone would not give us. The words 'I gave my daughter to the man' show the Torah trusts the father's statement. That makes the word לאיש necessary.

keyTerms.meaning: It was needed
For the teaching of רב הונא
Believed to make forbidden

steps.whyThisMatters: The father's word alone can make his daughter forbidden as a married woman, and this rule comes straight from the Torah.

phrases.english: Rather, where the verse is needed
is for what Rav Huna said in the name of Rav.
For Rav Huna said in the name of Rav:
From where do we know that a father is believed
to make his daughter forbidden, from the Torah?
As it says: 'I gave my daughter to the man.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי אִיצְטְרִיךְ קְרָא, לְכִדְרַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12 by giving the פסוק a different purpose.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the פסוק to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק is the source for הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק teaches that a father is believed to make his daughter forbidden, which logic alone would not teach.

steps.title: Then why does the verse add the word 'this'?
steps.stepSummary: Now that only 'to the man' is used for רב הונא's teaching, the גמרא asks what the extra word הזה is for.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need the word 'this'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices a leftover word. If the פסוק's point is only the father's trust, the word 'this' seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אסי had used הזה for 'permitting her.' Since that idea now comes from logic, the word הזה has no job. The גמרא expects every word of the Torah to teach something.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it?
'This' — the extra word in the פסוק

phrases.english: Why do I need 'this'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from step 13's answer, which left the word הזה without a job.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word הזה in the פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once הפה שאסר comes from logic, the word הזה that רב אסי used for it seems extra.

steps.title: 'This' teaches רבי יונה's rule: not a יבם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that הזה is needed for רבי יונה's teaching: 'this man,' and not a יבם. The laws of this section do not apply to a יבם.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for what רבי יונה taught. For רבי יונה taught: 'I gave my daughter to this man' — 'this,' and not to the יבם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the word הזה its own job, using a teaching of רבי יונה. This closes the discussion of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is part of the section about a husband who slanders his wife. The word הזה limits that section to the man the father gave her to. It does not include a יבם, who married her through יבום.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed for
A brother-in-law who marries his brother's widow

steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר comes from logic. The word לאיש teaches that a father is believed to make his daughter forbidden (רב הונא in the name of רב). The word הזה teaches that these laws do not apply to a יבם (רבי יונה).

phrases.english: It is needed for what Rabbi Yona taught.
For Rabbi Yona taught:
'I gave my daughter to this man.'
'This' — and not to the yavam.
phrases.notes: This פסוק is about a husband who slanders his wife, and those laws don't apply to a יבם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 14 by finding a separate teaching for the word הזה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning the extra word to a separate teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word הזה seems unnecessary once הפה שאסר comes from logic.
steps.terutzMaskana: הזה teaches that the laws of this section apply only to the husband and not to a יבם.

steps.title: A woman who said 'married' then 'single' is believed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a woman who first says she is an אשת איש and then says she is a פנויה is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A woman who said 'I am a married woman,' and then said 'I am unmarried,' is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a new case. A woman first says she is married and then says she is single, and the ברייתא says we believe her second statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a new topic: can a person take back a statement that made something forbidden? The ruling seems surprising, because her first statement should have made her forbidden to all men. That surprise sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: A married woman, forbidden to all other men
An unmarried woman, free to marry
She is believed

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
The woman who said "I am a married woman,"
and then went back and said "I am unmarried"
she is believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic. It shares a theme with הפה שאסר (steps 9-15), since in both cases a person changes what they said about a woman's status.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who said she was married and then said she was single is believed.

steps.title: Didn't she already make herself forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: by saying she was married, she made herself a חתיכה דאיסורא, so how can she undo it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't she make herself a 'piece of prohibition'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling of step 16. Once she said 'I am married,' she made herself forbidden, so how can her new words make her permitted?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of חתיכה דאיסורא says that a person who declares something forbidden for himself cannot later take it back. Her first statement locked her in as forbidden to all men. Her second statement looks like an attempt to take back her own words.

keyTerms.meaning: She made herself (by her own words)
A 'piece of prohibition': something a person declared forbidden for himself and cannot take back

phrases.english: But didn't she make herself
a "piece of prohibition"?
phrases.notes: He means: by her own words she made herself forbidden, like a piece of food someone declared not kosher for himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling of step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that she is believed when she says 'I am unmarried'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Her first statement made her a חתיכה דאיסורא for herself, and someone cannot cancel a prohibition they placed on themselves.

steps.title: She gave a good reason for her first words
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב הונא explains that the ברייתא is talking about a woman who gave an אמתלא, a believable reason for why she first said she was married.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב הונא said: The case is where she gave a reason for her words.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רב הונא answers the challenge. The ברייתא is talking about a woman who explained why she said 'I am married' at first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once she gives a believable reason for her first statement, it is no longer seen as a real declaration that she is forbidden. It turns out it was never a true claim, so there is no חתיכה דאיסורא to undo. Without such a reason, the challenge would stand.

keyTerms.meaning: A believable reason or explanation for why someone said something
Such as; the case is where

steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of אמתלא becomes the key to the whole section. It decides when a person may take back a statement that made something forbidden.

phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Huna said:
Such as where she gave a reason for her words.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא בַּר רַב הוּנָא כְּגוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to believe her in every case, even though her first words made her forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: She is believed only when she gives an אמתלא for her first statement.

steps.title: Another ברייתא says the same thing
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא spells out both sides: without an אמתלא she is not believed, and with an אמתלא she is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: If she said 'I am a married woman,' and then said 'I am unmarried,' she is not believed. But if she gave a reason for her words, she is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that supports רבא בר רב הונא. It openly makes the same split between having a reason and not having one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא says directly what רבא בר רב הונא had to explain. With no reason, her first words stand and she stays forbidden. With an אמתלא, she is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא brought as support)
She is not believed

steps.confusionAlert: Don't be thrown off: the first ברייתא (step 16) said 'believed' and this one says 'not believed' for the same words. There is no argument between them. This ברייתא simply shows that step 16 was talking about a woman who gave an אמתלא.

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
If she said "I am a married woman,"
and then went back and said "I am unmarried"
she is not believed.
And if she gave a reason for her words
she is believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 18.
steps.raayaObject: רבא בר רב הונא's explanation that she is believed only with an אמתלא
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that openly makes the split between a woman with an אמתלא and a woman without one

steps.title: The story of the beautiful woman
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with a story. A beautiful woman told unsuitable suitors that she was already betrothed, and later she accepted קידושין from a suitable man, explaining why she had said it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was also a story about an important woman who was very beautiful, and men rushed to betroth her. She said to them, 'I am betrothed.' Some time later she went and got herself betrothed. The חכמים asked her, 'Why did you do this?' She told them, 'At first, when unsuitable men came to me, I said I was betrothed. Now that suitable men have come, I went and got myself betrothed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a real story that shows an אמתלא in action. The woman's explanation is her reason for her earlier false claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She had made herself forbidden by saying 'I am betrothed,' yet later she married. Her explanation, that she only wanted to get rid of unworthy suitors, is exactly the kind of believable reason that lets her take back her first words.

keyTerms.meaning: Men rushed eagerly at her (to marry her)
Betrothed (has received קידושין)
Suitable, proper, decent people
What did you see? Why did you do this?

phrases.english: And there was also a story about one important woman
who was outstanding in beauty,
and people rushed at her to betroth her.
And she said to them: "I am betrothed."
Some time later she went and got herself betrothed.
The Sages said to her:
What did you see to do this?
She said to them:
At first, when there came to me
men who were not proper,
I said: "I am betrothed."
Now that proper men have come to me,
I went and got myself betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא of step 19 with a real-life example of an אמתלא.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that an אמתלא lets a woman take back 'I am married/betrothed'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story in which a woman's explanation (getting rid of unworthy suitors) was accepted

steps.title: The חכמים in אושא rule: with a reason, she is believed
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא שר הבירה brought this case to the חכמים in אושא, and they ruled that if she gave an אמתלא, she is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: This הלכה was brought by רב אחא שר הבירה before the חכמים in אושא, and they said: If she gave a reason for her words, she is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by reporting the official ruling of the חכמים in אושא. With an אמתלא, she is believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story is not just a one-time event. It was brought before the great court in אושא, which turned it into a set הלכה. This closes the discussion that began in step 16.

keyTerms.meaning: Brought up (presented a case for a ruling)
Officer of the capital (a title for רב אחא)
אושא, a town where the חכמים gathered

steps.whatToRemember: A woman who said 'I am married' and then 'I am single' is not believed, unless she gives an אמתלא, a believable reason for her first statement. Then she is believed.

phrases.english: And this halacha was brought up by
Rav Acha, officer of the capital,
before the Sages in Usha,
and they said:
If she gave a reason for her words
she is believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְזוֹ הֲלָכָה הֶעֱלָה רַב אַחָא שַׂר הַבִּירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story with a formal ruling of the חכמים.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If she gave an אמתלא for her first statement, she is believed when she says she is unmarried.

steps.title: שמואל asks about 'impure' then 'pure'
steps.stepSummary: שמואל asks רב about a woman who said 'I am טמאה' and then said 'I am טהורה.' What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל asked רב: If she said 'I am impure,' and then said 'I am pure,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל asks רב a new question. Does the same idea apply when a woman first says she is טמאה and then says she is טהורה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case is like the married/single case, but about טומאה instead of marriage. The question is whether her first words made her a חתיכה דאיסורא to her husband, or whether she can take them back as before.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked of him (a real question asked to a teacher)
Impure, here a נדה who is forbidden to her husband
Pure, permitted to her husband
What is the law?

phrases.english: Shmuel asked Rav:
If she said "I am impure,"
phrases.notes: She means she is a נדה, so she is forbidden to her husband.

phrases.english: and then went back and said "I am pure,"
what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the חתיכה דאיסורא / אמתלא discussion into a new area: נדה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can a woman who said 'I am טמאה' take it back by saying 'I am טהורה'?

steps.title: רב answers: here too, if she gives a reason
steps.stepSummary: רב begins to answer that in this case too, if she gives an אמתלא, she is believed. The answer continues on the next daf.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: Even in this case, if she gave [a reason for her words, she is believed]...
steps.whatsHappening: רב starts his answer to שמואל. He uses the same אמתלא rule as before, and the sentence finishes on the next page.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'even' (אף) tells us רב treats the טומאה case just like the married/single case. A believable reason lets her take back her first statement here too.

keyTerms.meaning: Even in this case too

phrases.english: He said to him:
Even in this case,
if she gave
phrases.notes: The sentence keeps going on the next page: 'a reason for her words, she is believed.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers שמואל's question from step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Just as with 'married' and 'single,' if she gives an אמתלא she is believed (the answer finishes on the next daf).
